description: Team 2Bits unites developers and researchers in AI, combustion physics, and aerospace data informatics. We built Project Pyros to bridge 20+ years of NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) microgravity data with deterministic physics scaling laws. Our platform predicts fire behavior for Artemis Moon bases (0.166g) and Mars habitats (0.38g), eliminating AI hallucinations with real fluid mechanics while tracking life-saving Earth firefighting spinoffs.
summary:
PROJECT PYROS (Predictive Yield & Risk in Orbital Spacefire) is an SI-powered, web-based dashboard and 3D WebGL simulation platform that transforms NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) combustion database into actionable fire safety intelligence for human space exploration.

The platform summarizes, ranks, and interprets all 22 relevant PSI combustion investigations — spanning gaseous (ACME/BRE, E-FIELD, CFI-G), liquid (FLEX, FLEX-2, CFI), solid (BASS, BASS-II, Saffire I–III), and aerosol (SAME, SAME-R, DAFT, DAFT-2) experiments — across four interactive 3D environments: an ISS orbital laboratory, an Artemis lunar base, a Martian pressurized rover, and a Mars surface outpost. Users can explore investigation dossiers, compare experimental variables side-by-side, and trace hardware lineages (CIR → ACME/MDCA, MSG → SPICE duct, SAME → DAFT instrument repurposing).

Because no partial-gravity combustion data yet exists in PSI, PROJECT PYROS implements deterministic physics bounding - Roper flame-height scaling, Grash of convection velocity, and Dalton oxygen partial-pressure laws — to extrapolate flammability between 0g (ISS) and 1g (Earth) for lunar (0.166g, 34% O₂, 10.2 psi) and Martian (0.38g) regimes. The platform also highlights terrestrial spinoffs including fine-water-mist extinguishers, dual-wavelength smoke detectors, and firefighter protective gear derived directly from spaceflight research.
details:
What does our project do?

When we first looked at NASA's PSI combustion database, we understood the challenge immediately — there's an incredible wealth of microgravity fire research spanning two decades, but it's scattered across dozens of investigations, different hardware platforms, and varying test conditions. A researcher trying to figure out "what happens if a fire starts inside an Artemis lunar habitat?" would have to manually dig through experiments that used completely different fuels, sensors, and atmospheric setups. We wanted to change that.

So we built PROJECT PYROS — a web-based dashboard paired with four immersive 3D simulation environments that take all 22 relevant PSI combustion investigations and make them searchable, comparable, and genuinely understandable.

On the dashboard side, users can browse every investigation with rich detail cards showing what fuels were tested, what shapes and sizes the samples were, what oxygen levels and pressures were used, what sensors captured the data, and what the scientists actually found. You can pull up any two investigations side by side and instantly see what they share, where they differ, and how they connect through shared hardware — like how the same smoke detection instrument from the SAME experiment was later repurposed to measure lunar dust in the DAFT studies. That kind of connection is nearly impossible to spot when you're reading individual papers, but our knowledge graph (which maps 352 relationships between investigations) surfaces it automatically.

The really fun part is the 3D simulations. We built four interactive environments in Three.js that let you actually experience fire behavior in the places astronauts will live and work:

  • Inside the ISS, you can watch a candle flame transform from its normal flickering teardrop shape into the eerie blue sphere that forms in microgravity — and it's not just an animation. There's a real Navier-Stokes fluid solver running on your GPU computing how removing gravity eliminates buoyant convection and forces combustion to rely purely on molecular diffusion. You can adjust the oxygen level, cabin pressure, and airflow speed with sliders and see the flame respond in real time.
  • On the Moon, we modeled an Artemis base camp at Shackleton Crater with habitation modules, solar arrays, and fuel cells. The challenge specifically mentions that the Moon Base will operate at roughly 10.2 psi and 34% oxygen to reduce spacesuit pre-breathing time — so we built that exact atmosphere into the simulation. You can toggle between five viewing modes including a thermal camera view and an emergency power failure scenario.
  • Inside a Mars rover, we recreated the Warm Electronics Box — the sealed avionics bay where a circuit failure could spark a fire under Martian partial gravity (0.38g). A guided 7-stage timeline walks you through how thermal overstress leads to micro-arcing, then polymer ignition, and finally autonomous safe mode shutdown.
  • On the Martian surface, you can trigger an emergency hypoxic venting protocol — dumping the habitat's breathable atmosphere into Mars's near-vacuum (0.13% oxygen) and watching the flame extinguish in under 2.5 seconds. It's a vivid demonstration of how Mars's hostile atmosphere could actually be used as a fire suppression tool.

How does it address the challenge?

The challenge says PSI data is "hard to find, harder to compare, and harder yet to interpret." We tackled all three directly.

Finding is solved by our Investigation Explorer — search by fuel type, hardware facility, fire safety pillar (prevention, detection, or suppression), or just scroll through organized dossier cards. No more hunting through NASA's raw database.

Comparing is solved by our cross-investigation comparison engine and knowledge graph. Select any two experiments and get an instant breakdown: shared hardware lineage, overlapping test conditions, differing fuel types, and synthesized scientific insights. The graph captures every connection the challenge mentions — ACME's six gaseous fuel experiments sharing CIR hardware, FLEX/FLEX-2/CFI sharing the MDCA droplet apparatus, BASS/BASS-II/SPICE/SLICE sharing the MSG flow duct, and the SAME-to-DAFT instrument evolution.

Interpreting is solved by our deterministic physics engine. The challenge notes that no partial-gravity combustion data currently exists in PSI, but suggests that microgravity and normal-gravity results could bound intermediate gravity levels. That's exactly what we implemented. Using Roper flame-height scaling, Grashof convection analysis, and Dalton's partial pressure law, our engine calculates what happens to flame height, spread rate, and convection velocity at any gravity between 0g and 1g — with honest confidence levels that flag where predictions need future LUCI and FM2 data to be refined.

Users can type natural scenario queries like "What happens during a fabric fire in a lunar habitat at 34% O₂?" and get a ranked list of the most relevant PSI investigations, computed physics bounds, and specific safety recommendations — all grounded in real NASA data with zero hallucinated content.

Why does this matter?

Fire in space is not a theoretical concern — it's a documented killer. The Apollo 1 crew died in a pure-oxygen fire. Apollo 13 nearly lost its crew to an oxygen tank explosion. The Mir station crew survived a terrifying chemical fire that filled their station with toxic smoke. As we prepare to send astronauts back to the Moon and eventually to Mars, understanding fire behavior in these alien environments isn't just academic — it's life or death.

The twist is that lunar and Martian habitats will operate at elevated oxygen concentrations (30-34% O₂) to make spacesuit pre-breathing practical, which means materials that are perfectly safe on Earth become significantly more flammable. Our platform helps researchers, engineers, and students quickly understand which NASA experiments are most relevant to these new environments and what the physics tells us about fire risks we haven't directly tested yet.

We also highlight how space fire research has already saved lives on Earth — lightweight composite breathing tanks that replaced 35-pound steel cylinders for firefighters, dual-wavelength smoke detectors that cut false alarms in mines by 85%, and heat-resistant Nomex and PBI fabrics used in every modern firefighter's turnout coat. These spinoffs deserve to be visible and accessible.

What did we build it with?

We kept the frontend deliberately simple — vanilla JavaScript with ES modules, no React, no build tools, no npm install required. The 3D scenes run on Three.js 0.170.0 with a custom GPU-accelerated fluid physics solver that auto-detects WebGPU support and falls back to WebGL2 so it works on any modern browser. The entire frontend, including the complete 22-investigation dataset, is embedded and works fully offline — no server required.

The backend is Python with FastAPI serving a RESTful API, NetworkX for the knowledge graph, NumPy for physics computations, and an optional LangChain + FAISS RAG pipeline for enhanced natural language queries (with Google Gemini or OpenAI). Pydantic enforces strict data validation on every investigation record.

What makes it creative?

Honestly, we're most proud of the "zero mockup" principle. Every single number in the platform — every oxygen percentage, every flame height prediction, every sensor name, every atmospheric test condition — comes from authentic NASA PSI data or verified physics equations. We built an autonomous fallback system so that even if the LLM is unavailable, the dashboard still delivers scientifically accurate, peer-reviewed answers through a grounded cache and deterministic solver. A built-in Criteria Audit modal lets anyone verify this with a single click.

We also thought carefully about accessibility. A professor can use the Investigation Explorer as a teaching tool. A graduate student can run scenario queries to scope their thesis research. An aerospace engineer can compute physics bounds for habitat design. And anyone can just explore the 3D environments and develop an intuitive feel for why fire behaves so differently without gravity — something that's almost impossible to convey through papers and data tables alone.
